Entertainment.title: Celebrity Traitors, episode eight: Series left on a knife edge after a trip to the field of screams
Entertainment.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode eight of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Original Celebrity Traitor Maya Jama, latest recruit King Kenny and now even the reluctant James Acaster - hooray! - have developed a real appetite for murder this week.

And going into Friday's episode we knew that their collective cruel intention was to see that one of three faithfuls, Miranda Hart, Romesh Ranganathan or Sebastian "Bash" Croft, did not make it to breakfast.

When it became clear that the murdered Miranda had danced her last dance in the castle - leaving only 10 of the initial 21 players - the pressure began to mount and speculation was rife as to whodunnit and why?

The self-declared Miss Marple wannabe had been stitched up, of course. "Miranda is a good detective," noted James A in a flashback to the turret talk from the night before.

"I don't know who I'm becoming," responded Maya - who has taken to treachery like a duck to water - "but I feel it in my loins, and Miranda is the only one that makes sense."

Miranda, who had been in her element sleuthing away on the show, did not take the news of her untimely death at all well, throwing her murder note to the ground. "No! Absolutely not," she cried.

"Oh bottoms!

"I'm so cross with myself, I was wholly focusing on my Joanne issue," she added, with reference to her theory about Joanne McNally being a traitor. One that even Miranda herself had - unwisely - "debunked" at the roundtable.

Ending on a more positive note, the comedian, who has had health issues in recent years, reflected: "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary that I've been able to get back and do the thing that I love professionally and do the things that I love personally.

"Like wandering around a Scottish island and being in nature and laughing and connecting. There were times that I didn't think that would be possible again".

With Miss Marple now out of the picture, James A told viewers that two of the remaining traitor hunters, James Blunt and Michael Sheen are like "Holmes and Watson".

"Luckily they're completely looking in all the wrong places," he added.

Leigh-Anne, having lost her new Big Mix dance partner from episode six, said she was now praying that the heat on her would now cool down.

While Miranda was being murdered on Thursday night, out in the real world another Little Mix star Jade Thirlwell told BBC News - at the Mercury prize ceremony - that her groupmate was a real life "faithful through and through".

Those kind words would be worth little if the now nicely positioned traitors kept going at this rate, however.

"This is actually embarrassing," declared comedian Romesh at breakfast.

"We are getting battered," a sneaky Maya agreed. "This is just getting harder and harder by the second."

Wink, wink.

Breaking character in the safety of the diary room, the Gentleman actress and presenter admitted: "I'm not gonna lie, I feel terrible about Miranda, I really do and she will be sorely missed.

"But with great honour comes great pressure, and here I am, ’OG Traits‘, still flying it up."

Joanne had earlier joked that Maya would not be killed or banished as "she's too hot. The hot ones always survive."

After breakfast, James B, who has been pretty consistently wrong with his theories throughout the series, continued his fine form, saying of Maya and Kenny: "I think they are the two most innocent."

He joked (it was a joke, right?): "Watching me in this castle must be like watching Sherlock at work."

With less heat on her than Christmas Day in Blackpool, Maya started planting a seed that roundtable "chief investigator" Michael Sheen might be up to something.

"How has that guy not been killed?" asked Romesh.

"It's like not getting rid of [Hercule] Poirot," he added, as the literary detective references kept coming.

Michael and Sharon - fast becoming a dark horse with her theory about Ross Kemp having been killed with perfume - said she was determined to catch a traitor and would "not be taking any prisoners".

On to Friday's mission, as the dwindling group arrived in a "field of screams", as presenter Claudia Winkleman aptly put it, full of scary-looking scarecrows.

"This is like the Wickerman," said Joanne. "A solo scarecrow is sinister enough. A gaggle of scarecrows is terrifying."

The task involved them attempting to retrieve bags of gold from inside the straw men with a pitchfork, in a bid to add thousands of pounds to the charity prize pot.

Joanne's knot-tying badge she claimed to have been awarded in her youth didn't seem to help her much, though, as she struggled initially to grab any gold.

"I have a newfound respect for the farming community," she declared.

But it wasn't only gold on offer, it transpired. An as-yet unrevealed game-changing power would be bestowed upon one player, but only after they had to blow up the proxy pumpkin scarecrow heads of all but three of the most trustworthy contestants.

Things got a bit awkward when poor Sharon "got so mad at the boys" - James B, Michael and Kenny - over which heads should roll.

In the most remarkably stupid moment of the series since Richard E Grant told everyone he was a traitor, the group chose to preserve the heads belonging to Maya, James A and Kenny.

"I had to hold in my laughter," said Maya, privately afterwards. "Of all people, you saved us. I just thought, 'oh my gosh, have we completed this game already? We are trusting. We are unsuspecting. We are killing you all'."

With the others en route back to the castle, Winkleman quipped to the traitors: "This is like an outdoor turret."

The special power was revealed to be a double dagger enabling "the trustworthy trio", as James A is now calling them, to award two banishment votes to whoever they wanted to hold it.

King Kenny became King Arthur being crowned keeper of the special blade.

"I think it's in the right hands," declared James B back at the castle, now colder than ever in terms of catching a traitor.

"I feel like whoever it is, they are five steps ahead of us," noted a befuddled Leigh-Anne. "We don't have a clue!"

Romesh then had to remind Joanne that her policy of not voting off Michael because he's "great company" is not really how the game should work.

With the double dagger in play and time running out for the faithful, Michael declared that he had to catch a traitor tonight.

As discussions began, double trouble Kenny warned: "Be nice to me everyone!"

"You're a powerful man," noted Joanne.

Bash, who had flown under the radar until this point, drew some heat along with Leigh-Anne and Sharon at another roundtable led my Don Michael.

"If you're a faithful, why are you still here?" Bash asked the Welshman, who noted he had a shield last time out.

Romesh agreed: "I definitely would have killed you by now if I was a traitor. And I mean that as a massive compliment, because I think, for the morale of the group, you not being here would decimate us."

In an attempt to deflect attention away from himself, Michael stressed how Sharon had been acting like a "totally different person" of late.

Kenny bought it, sticking his double dagger into the Barbie actress. And James B voted the same way due to her "suspicious" actions earlier on.

Scotswoman Sharon received four votes, along with Irish comic Joanne, meaning that - after desperate final pleas from the pair - it went to second round.

"Do whatever youse want, it's a game," offered a seemingly defeated Sharon.

"I wish I didn't take this dagger," said Kenny, ahead of his decisive second thrust of the double blade. "But I'm gonna vote for..."

The producers then left things, quite literally, on a knife edge.

Ten contestant remain (for now): seven faithfuls (soon to be six) and three traitors, putting the cloaked interlopers in a great position going into the final two episodes.

With the hurly-burly done for another week, we will wait with baited breath until Hallowe'en's double header to see how the battle will be lost and won.

Entertainment.title: James Bond: Jack Lowden and Callum Turner to screen test this weekend, reports say
Entertainment.text:
Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O'Connor are among the actors thought to be taking part in final auditions to play James Bond, according to reports.

Screen tests are said to be taking place this weekend, possibly as early as Friday, according to the Hollywood Reporter, external, with between three and five actors understood to have reached the last stages of the process.

The finalists are said to be taking part in auditions with three components - stunts, camera presence and dialogue.

Deadline reported the screen tests, external had been due take place in early October, but had been delayed by scheduling conflicts, while Variety said Turner and Lowden, external "appear to be in the mix" to replace Daniel Craig.

British actors Aaron Taylor-Johnson and James Norton were previously connected to the role, while Irish actor Paul Mescal's name had also been thrown into the mix.

Other actors now appear to be in the frame, but reports on the current casting situation vary.

Variety suggested Slow Horses star Lowden may now be edging ahead, while Masters of the Air star Turner was speculated about earlier this year, with some fans suggesting his wife Dua Lipa could sing the Bond theme song.

Sources told Deadline that at least four final screen test offers have been made, and while unconfirmed, "three of the four expected to test are Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O'Connor".

O'Connor is best known for playing Prince Charles in The Crown, and for starring in 2025's Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery, with Craig.

Jack O'Connell had been thought to be in the mix, but sources said this may no longer be the case, while Euphoria and Wuthering Heights Star Jacob Elordi is not thought to be testing.

Other stars who were previously linked with the role include The King's Man star Harris Dickinson, along with SAS: Rogue Heroes' Jack Barton.

Deadline said: "Even with the tests wrapping next week, there is no timeline for when a final decision will be made."

Amazon MGM Studios, who now control the Bond franchise, announced in May, external that the casting process was under way, but had no further comment at the time.

In August, Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, told Deadline, external the "end of the year is a good bet" for possible news on who would be playing Bond.

"We are being really, really methodical. Having worked with Barbara Broccoli at the studio, I mean, Daniel Craig is a hard act to follow," she said.

"And it's got to be something really different that is a stirring and exciting and different."

The BBC's Lizo Mzimba reported in September that "for a series where the stakes are so high, no expense is spared in ensuring that the film team know exactly how each auditionee will come across on screen".

He added: "As the 007 team themselves have explained, external in the past: 'Bond screen tests are elaborate affairs involving hair and make-up, costumes, sets, and other actors'."

The next James Bond: The (00)7 questions fans want answered

Search for new James Bond officially kicks off as auditions begin

Only six actors have ever played novelist Ian Fleming's British Secret Service agent 007 in the official film series - Sean Connery, Roger Moore, George Lazenby, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig.

The last announcement of a new Bond was in 2005 with Craig, who last starred in the role in 2021's No Time to Die, directed by Cary Joji Fukunaga.

During the equivalent stage of the audition process two decades ago, Superman actor Henry Cavill was widely thought to have also been in the running.

"They told me I was close," Cavill told the Happy Sad Confused podcast in 2022. "They told me it was ultimately down to, and this is what I've been told, it was just down to me and Daniel, and I was the younger option.

"They obviously went with Daniel and I think it was an amazing choice to go with Daniel," he said. "I probably wasn't ready at the time and I think Daniel did an incredible job over the past movies, so I'm happy they made that choice."

The forthcoming film, reportedly out in 2028, will be directed by Dune's Denis Villeneuve, with Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight writing the script.

Knight told Zoe Ball on Greatest Hits Radio, external in September that the first draft of the script was completed.

Amazon bought MGM for $8.5bn (£6.3bn) in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond, and they are reported to have paid at least $20m (£14.9m) more for the rights to creatively control Bond's future.

Pascal and David Heyman are producing the film, while Tanya Lapointe is executive producer.

Knight's final words on the film were about how much he was enjoying working on it.

He told Ball:, external "I'm absolutely loving doing it. It's an honour to be asked. And believe it's going to be so good. I really do believe it's going to be amazing."

Entertainment.title: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope
Entertainment.text:
Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her show-stopping second album This Music May Contain Hope.

A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood glamour, it beat the likes of Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean and Jade to scoop the £25,000 prize.

"I couldn't tell you how grateful I am to be holding this," said Raye, clutching her trophy at Newcastle's Utilita Arena. "I'm shaking, I'm jet-lagged, I'm tired. It's all blurry."

It is the first time a pop album has won the coveted prize - which recognises the best British or Irish album of the last 12 months - since M People's Elegant Slumming in 1994.

Speaking to the BBC afterwards, Raye said she'd "poured everything I had" into the record, which features the global hit song Where Is My Husband?

"I made this album not focusing on commercial [success], not focusing on making things cookie-cutter," said the 28-year-old.

"Some of these songs are seven minutes. They're indulgent. They're maximalist."

Across 17 tracks and 73 minutes, the record tells a cinematic story about a relationship that ends in tears on the rainy streets of Paris, then follows our plucky heroine as she dusts off the debris and emerges stronger and more resilient.

Along the way, it features both of her grandparents, the soul legend Al Green, four separate orchestras and more than 100 musicians.

But the album almost never happened. Two years ago this week, the singer's car was stolen, along with all of her songwriting notebooks and demos.

Although they were eventually recovered, it delayed work on This Music May Contain Hope by almost a year.

Looking back, she was philosophical about the delay.

"I was distraught. I was very worried, but you know, it all turned out great.

"Every little slip, every little accident, every little thing, it creates the path that you take.

"And it's easy to spend time wishing things were the other way. But right now, I certainly do not."

Entertainment.title: Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton
Entertainment.text:
The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize.

During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize.

As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa, to cheers and gasps from the audience.

They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet".

The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films.

William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.

There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives £1m.

The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November.

Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro.

The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability.

At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible".

Entertainment.title: Tom Skerritt, star of Top Gun and Alien, dies aged 93
Entertainment.text:
US actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in the TV series Picket Fences and the films Alien and Top Gun, has died aged 93, his family says.

Skerritt died on Wednesday of natural causes, his family said, adding: "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humour, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives."

In a six-decade career, he appeared in the film Mash, A River Runs Through It and Ted. He also co-founded TheFilmSchool in Seattle to support next-generation filmmakers and storytellers.

His family said he will be remembered "for his belief that stories can help people heal, find purpose and create change".

The moustachioed star of several 20th Century hit films was born in 1933 in Detroit, Michigan, and served in the US Air Force before pursuing an acting career that boasted several military roles.

He made his film debut in 1962 alongside a young Robert Redford ​in War Hunt and years later reunited with Redford in the 1992 period drama A River Runs Through It, which starred Brad Pitt.

Skerritt's breakthrough role came when he played US army surgeon Duke Forrest in the 1970 Korean War comedy Mash, which also starred Donald Sutherland, Elliott Gould and Sally Kellerman.

The hit film, which was released amid unrest over the Vietnam War, was nominated for five Academy Awards and was adapted for television two years later.

He also starred alongside Sigourney Weaver in the 1979 sci-fi film Alien, which earned two Oscar nominations, and led to three sequels and several crossover projects.

"It is spontaneity and impulse ​that make the difference, and that is ⁠what I felt we had with 'Alien'," Skerritt said in a 2019 interview, according to news agency Reuters.

"Every one of us had that immediate rapport with each other."

Skerritt said that one of the things he liked most when he first read the script was that "the woman becomes a hero", referring to Weaver's character, Ripley.

During his career, he starred opposite several strong female leads.

He appeared with Shirley MacLaine in the 1977 film Turning Point and played Sally Field's husband in 1989's Steel Magnolias.

As Cdr Mike "Viper" Metcalf in the 1986 classic Top Gun, the versatile actor appeared alongside a young Tom Cruise.

On television, he won an Emmy Award in 1993 for his role as Sheriff Jimmy Brock in David E Kelley's drama Picket Fences.

The quirky procedural's ensemble cast was nominated for Sag Awards in 1995 and 1996 and he received a nod for male actor in a drama series in 1995.

Lauren Holly, who played Skerritt's deputy on Picket Fences, described him in a tribute as "our leader".

"His example made those years such a joy and we all loved and respected him so much," Holly wrote.

"He cared deeply for his family - both the one at home and the one at work. He cared deeply for his planet and all of its inhabitants. He had a huge impact on my life and so many memories I have of him include sharing fits of crippling laughter."

Skerritt also had guest roles on the small screen in The West Wing, Madam Secretary, Law & Order: SVU and Huff. He reteamed with Field as the family patriarch, William Walker, in the drama Brothers & Sisters from 2007-09.

Entertainment.title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
Entertainment.text:
A US judge has ordered Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Trump cancelled a previous deposition - an interview under oath - on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance".

But a lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia that day and had "prioritised that" over answering their questions.

Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is in the phase known as "discovery", in which the two sides provide internal or other records that could form evidence.

Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, told a court in Miami on Thursday that with two months left in the discovery period, Trump had still not completed a deposition.

US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett said Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December or face sanctions - the most extreme of which could be the dismissal of the lawsuit - unless the discovery period is extended.

In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings. Depositions carry legal weight - they are recorded verbatim by a court reporter and the transcripts can later be used as evidence in trials.

They typically take place in a lawyer's office without a judge physically present.

In defamation cases, lawyers for both sides are normally present for depositions.

Last week, lawyers asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place.

On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his Mar-a-Lago property in Florida.

In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year and claimed the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action".

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

In July, Trump's lawyers conceded they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC Select or through US broadcasters.

Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, the broadcaster's commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".

Entertainment.title: Stratford's Matilda celebrates 15 years as West End success story
Entertainment.text:
A musical that began life as a Christmas production in Stratford-upon-Avon has become one of the biggest theatre successes of the century as it celebrates 15 years in London's West End.

Matilda The Musical, which is now the 10th longest-running musical in West End history, has been seen by more than 12 million people around the world, staged more than 10,000 performances and played in more than 100 cities.

Composer and lyricist Tim Minchin said he was still amazed by the show's success.

"Probably the biggest family musical of this century is written by [us] couple of idiots," he joked.

Based on Roald Dahl's classic children's novel, the production premiered at the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon in 2010 before transferring to the West End the following year.

Written by Dennis Kelly, with music and lyrics by Minchin, the musical has gone on to win more than 100 international awards, including 25 for best musical.

Kelly said neither of them expected the production to become a global phenomenon.

"If we'd made a successful show at Stratford, we'd have been delighted," he said.

"I just remember the first night... the audience going crazy and I just wasn't ready for it all.

"I was standing at the back, I wasn't even sitting in a seat and I just wasn't ready for it and I just thought, 'This is weird'."

Jacqui O'Hanlon, deputy executive director of the Royal Shakespeare Company, said nobody involved in the original production could have predicted its longevity.

"None of us could have guessed that it would be the global phenomenon that 16 years later we're still talking about," she said.

"We started the run of the show with ticket discounts in place for the previews, because there were seating gaps and by the end of it, tickets were being sold on eBay for hundreds of pounds, so it was that quick."

The show is currently touring the UK and Ireland while continuing its West End run, with tickets on sale in London until September 2027.

Entertainment.title: Call of Duty promises a return to form - but can it compete with GTA?
Entertainment.text:
Call of Duty is back - and it's got a lot to prove.

Last year was a low point for the video game juggernaut, with poor reviews for its single-player campaign mode and multiplayer fans defecting to rival titles.

So for latest instalment, Modern Warfare 4, publisher Activision is pulling out all the stops to bring fans back on board.

But with increasing competition for fans' time and attention, and the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 just weeks away, can Call of Duty still cut through?

BBC Newsbeat spoke to some of those behind the game to find out, and why they see the upcoming release of GTA 6 as an "opportunity".

Since 2009, Call of Duty has been at the top - or a close second-place - in the US video game sales charts every year.

But 2025's edition, Black Ops 7, dropped to seventh place in America, according to data from analytics firm Circana. In the UK, it was the eighth best-selling game, external.

It’s thought the game’s inclusion on Xbox’s Game Pass subscription service, where it won’t appear on release this year, hit sales.

But competition from long-running rival Battlefield 6 and new release Arc Raiders - a surprise success from Swedish studio Embark - put the behemoth on the back foot.

Fans also complained about the inclusion of novelty skins, which change the appearance of characters during multiplayer games, based on cartoons, external and other pop culture crossovers.

Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, admits it was a tough year for the series.

"I think we missed expectations with our community last year," he says.

"So we took a step back, we listened to them."

Players now have the ability to switch off controversial cosmetic changes, and Bahl says Modern Warfare 4 is a "return to form".

It's a message they've been keen to get out.

Newsbeat meets Bahl in a corner of Shoreditch, London, that's been turned into a convincing replica of a South Korean street complete with noodle bars and convenience stores.

It's inspired by Modern Warfare 4's storyline, which depicts a North Korean invasion - a decision that provoked a mixed reaction in the lead-up to release.

A similar installation to promote the game has been built in downtown LA - but it's far from the only extravagant promotional attempt to generate buzz around the game.

Back in July, Activision recruited Obsession star Inde Navarrette - who streamed Call of Duty on Twitch before becoming one of Hollywood's hottest young stars - to publicise the game at sports convention Fanatics Fest, external.

It's also struck a sponsorship deal with six-a-side football competition Baller League and worked with world's biggest YouTuber Mr Beast to showcase the game's new DMZ multiplayer mode, external.

Bahl says the events and collabs are designed to demonstrate Call of Duty's "stature, swagger and scale" - something he admits does not come cheap.

He says he's always thinking of ways for Call of Duty to leverage its position and "show up in culture in a really big and innovative way" to reach "as many people as possible".

Call of Duty does have some strong competition in that space, however.

This year it's launching just weeks before GTA 6 - arguably the most anticipated video game of the decade.

Despite rising console prices, there's hope that the massive interest in Rockstar Games' ultra-blockbuster will convince people to buy a new console or return to the hobby.

Bahl says GTA 6 and Call of Duty are "the two biggest games of the year" but they're not necessarily in direct competition.

"More people dusting off their Xbox or their PlayStation, starting to play for the first time, it gives an opportunity for more gamers to come in and play both of the games," says Bahl.

GTA 6 will only be released on PlayStation 5 and Xbox consoles at first, and multiplayer modes won't be available at launch.

"So we feel like this is differentiated enough to really stand out," says Bahl.

The game itself sells for about £70 in the UK, but Bahl points out it can be a year-round hangout space for many fans.

"The number one reason people come to Call of Duty is not just for the combat or the gunplay, but it's actually because their friends are there, right?

"And so that social connection is so powerful."

Entertainment.title: Traitor behaviour splits opinion as paranoia deepens
Entertainment.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode seven of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Six days is a long time in The Celebrity Traitors.

So it was a relief to be put out of our misery as last Friday's literal yawn-fest came to its slow-burning conclusion; the traitorous trio eventually succeeding in their mission to kill in plain sight.

The snoozefest - which involved reluctant traitor James Acaster making faithful Ross Kemp yawn by boring him to tears - meant the paranoid EastEnders star was finally put out of his misery.

On learning his fate, the actor turned to Shakespeare - who else?

"To thine own self be true," he declared, quoting Polonius from Hamlet.

As usual at breakfast, the faithfuls seated early mused over who may have been murdered overnight: "If Jerry's not here, I don't think I can handle it," Romesh Ranganathan confessed.

Jerry Hall was charmingly late to the party. After everyone had discussed Ross's demise, she piped up in her famous Texan drawl: "Is Ross gone?"

As the typical off-the-wall theories began to swirl, Jerry later told Miranda Hart she suspected fellow faithful James Blunt - for the very plausible reason that "his face is redder than a fox's ass at gooseberry time". It's as good a reason as any proffered so far this series.

Once the croissant crumbs had been cleared, it was time for a mission that threw the cat among the pigeons - not least because the traitor's lair it took place in "smelled like a litter tray", according to Jerry.

Miranda felt there were more complex olfactory notes at play: "A mix of salmon, cheap cologne and crotch." Delightful.

The mission involved each player having to build a shield on a plinth in front of them out of 3D jigsaw-type pieces which were buried in troughs in sawdust. Think Krypton Factor meets lucky dip.

At three intervals, a bell would ring, and the players all had to stop and put on blindfolds for a few minutes. The traitors could then remove theirs and go about sabotaging the handiwork of anyone they fancied.

And while James A revealed he was "starting to have more fun" after murdering poor Ross, if there was a prize for the worst traitor of all time, he would still smash it.

He was too scared to take off his blindfold and remove any shield pieces from the faithfuls, leaving the dirty work - and all the risk - to fellow traitors Maya Jama and King Kenny. Suffice to say, they were not impressed.

"He didn't even lift the blindfold off - I'm speechless," said Maya.

James A knew he was in trouble: "I'm aware I'll get a dressing down in the turret but I am the one who killed Grant Mitchell."

He wasn't wrong about the telling off. And the fact he completed his own puzzle, earning himself a shield, must have really riled his co-conspirators.

To be fair, you could argue he's playing a blinder - there's been very little suspicion of him so far.

Three other celebrities also managed to complete their shield puzzles - James B, Joanne McNall and Michael Sheen - but no money was banked after Maya and Kenny panicked and didn't remove any pieces at their last opportunity.

But the task at least threw up another bunch of mad theories for the faithfuls to chew over, as they tried to unsuccessfully guess where the floorboard creaking was coming from as two of the traitors tried to creep around the room.

It was good news for Romesh at least, whose hay fever saved the day - Sharon Rooney could hear him sniffing constantly next to her so knew he couldn't have been a traitor.

Maybe the tickly moustache isn't helping his allergies - and combing it won't make much difference.

Entertainment.title: At Rikers, Inmates See Themselves in a Film About America’s Jails
Entertainment.text:
As inmates at the Rikers Island jail complex filed into a gymnasium for a documentary screening last week, some in the front rows were buzzing from a recent basketball league win. Others shuffled between plastic chairs in search of conversation.

Few seemed to anticipate that within the hour, the matinee showing would leave several of them fighting back tears.

The film, “Crime and Punishment in America,” is set to premiere on Nov. 16 on PBS. In four parts, and across eight hours, it chronicles the history of the criminal justice system in the United States, dating to the colonial era. Told chronologically through archival materials and interviews with experts and people who were once incarcerated, the docuseries is both macroscopic and meticulous in its examination of how the nation has constructed its laws and the penalties for those who break them.

The film discusses the American origins of the modern penitentiary system (“Incarceration as both punishment and rehabilitation was something no country had ever tried”) and the legacies of slavery (“Most prisons were modeled on the New York system of private contractors and forced labor”). It also looks at the proliferation of “tough on crime” approaches to criminal justice policy: “In 50 states, in 3,000 counties, a series of actors, most of them unknown to us, made small decisions in the direction of harshness.”

“Throughout the course of that project, I just was constantly reminded of how little I knew — meaning nothing — about the history of the justice system, and why our prisons are the way they are,” Novick said. She was particularly interested in how the United States became one of the world’s leading incarcerators, invested in punishing criminals harshly and often inequitably. “We believe in redemption and forgiveness and mercy,” she said, “but not for everyone.”

In making “Crime and Punishment in America,” Novick added, she hoped to explore a fundamental question: “How did we get here?”

At Rikers, Novick couldn’t show the inmates all eight hours of her new film, so she screened a 48-minute clip reel instead. The beleaguered complex in the East River, with its history of violence and dysfunction, has been ordered to close by next August, though the city appears unlikely to meet that deadline. It ultimately plans to replace Rikers with four smaller borough-based jails.

Inmates watched the clips with rapt attention. In a discussion that followed, they were more open and emotional than Novick had expected.

They expressed weariness about inhumane conditions for inmates, frustration about apathy that sentencing judges can seem to show and sorrow about forces outside their control affecting their incarceration.

Joel Clapp, who had just recently been released from prison before being arrested again last month, spoke about his troubled upbringing, which he felt he could not overcome.

“Circumstances made us crash and burn,” Clapp said. “We didn’t know how to deal with it. We didn’t know how to reach out for help, because we continuously keep getting judged for our past over and over and over.”

Niko Willer agreed: “Once you come through, it becomes a revolving door,” he said. Willer, who in May was convicted of burglary, has been in and out of the carceral system since he was 9 years old.

When Stanley Richards, the commissioner of the New York City Department of Correction, took the microphone, he encouraged the inmates to be wary of becoming stuck in their vexation.

“Don’t let that anger be an anchor around your ankles,” said Richards, who is the first formerly incarcerated person to be the department’s commissioner. Having “hard conversations” about such feelings, he added, can become “a springboard of hope.”

Numerous inmates said they felt empowered both by the event, which they characterized as part of the rehabilitation support that had not always been available to those in jail, and by the fact that Richards himself had once been imprisoned. “Things have really got better,” said one inmate, Rohan Brown.

Rahsaan Thomas was held at Rikers several times in the late ’80s and early ’90s, at the same time that his mother and stepfather worked at the facility. He told the crowd that while serving a stint at the San Quentin prison complex in California, he became a writer, podcaster and filmmaker. (Thomas had been sentenced to 55 years and six months to life for a second-degree murder conviction and related charges, but California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, commuted that sentence.)

Thomas is now a consulting producer on Novick’s film, and appears in it. Some inmates recognized him onscreen.

“I was supposed to never come home,” he said.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Met Police confirms it received 2019 letter with "number of claims" about Meghan's father
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A letter making a "number of claims" relating to the Duchess of Sussex's father was received by the Metropolitan Police in 2019, Scotland Yard has confirmed.

The Met said it passed the information relating to allegations outside the UK to the office of the Duke and Duchess but did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.

It was reported on Friday that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Thomas Markle, 82, had been found in his former home in the Philippines. Markle, who is based in the US, denies possessing any such images.

On Friday, Meghan said she was informed about "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father in 2018. The Met said it was reviewing the matter and deciding whether to refer itself to the police watchdog.

Responding to Saturday's developments dating the letter to 2019, a spokesman for the duchess said "any discrepancy of a few months" was "an understandable consequence of that passage of time".

The claims were first carried by the Sun newspaper, which later said that the letter made direct allegations of child sex abuse against Markle.

In a statement, Scotland Yard said: "Following a thorough review of Met Police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.

"It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

"The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.

"The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach."

Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.

He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having a leg amputated in 2025.

Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home, the Sun reported.

He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the FBI in July.

In a statement released by Meghan on Friday she said that when she received the information of the claims against her father she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".

Meghan said she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

Authorities in the Philippines have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father.

The BBC was told on Friday the matter was being investigated by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force.

Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured his computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.

Meghan is the only daughter of Markle and her mother Doria Ragland.

He pulled out of attending Meghan and Harry's wedding in 2018 - citing ill health - and they became estranged.

The duke and duchess moved to the US in 2020 after stepping down as working royals.

They returned to the UK with their children this year after six years away.

BreakingNewsTab.title: British woman dies after trying to rescue sons swept away at sea in the Bahamas
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A British mum has died after attempting to rescue her two sons when they were swept away while snorkelling in the Bahamas.

The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an investigation into the sudden death of a 36-year-old British woman on Tuesday.

The force said it believed the woman - thought to be from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire - had been snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.

In an attempt to rescue her sons, "the woman was also swept away", police said. The children were subsequently rescued from the water.

In a statement, posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said: "According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.

"Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.

"Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.

"In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.

"She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered.

"Foul play is not suspected at this time.

"An autopsy will be conducted to assist in determining the exact cause of death."

A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.

"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

BreakingNewsTab.title: How to heat your home without turning on the heating
BreakingNewsTab.text:
As the UK braces for a chilly weekend, with powerful winds and heavy rain hitting parts of the country, people are looking for ways to bring some warmth to their homes without cranking up the heating just yet. It is autumn after all.

But with rising energy prices making heating homes more expensive, taking action now could pay off in the long run.

Experts warn, though, that if you're elderly or vulnerable you shouldn't compromise your health.

To help you prepare for the chillier months, BBC News asked families and experts to share their tips for keeping your home warm and cost-effective.

When it gets cold, many people turn to hot water bottles and blankets - but there are other ways to warm your body.

The British Heart Foundation recommends wearing lots of thin layers, rather than one thick layer, to trap the heat in.

Natalie, 29, says she's replaced some of the clothes she wears round the house with supermarket thermal leggings and tops and says "it's made such a difference".

Amber Waring, 27, from Devon, says she eats warm meals like stews and pasta bakes, and dances round the kitchen with her toddler while they cook to help keep warm.

With the clocks going back this weekend, the nights will be drawing in.

So if you have a thicker duvet, now is the time to bring it out. Some supermarkets sell winter duvets for under £20 - look for 10.5 tog or higher.

But there's something to be said for a craftily placed blanket, too. When it gets cold, Rebecca, 44, from Hertfordshire, sleeps with a blanket underneath her mattress, which she says stops draughts. "This was passed to me by my nan, she swore by it," she says. Others swear by placing a blanket above the mattress but under the bedsheet.

You can heat your bed before getting in with a hot water bottle, but make sure you check the expiry date. A guide by NHS Scotland, external says to let the water from the kettle cool for a few minutes before filling, only fill it two-thirds full, squeeze air out of the top before putting the stopper on, and don't hold it directly against your skin.

Using an electric blanket - to heat your bed before you get in or to wrap around yourself on the sofa - is "one of the cheapest ways" to stay warm, says Emily Seymour, energy editor at consumer organisation Which?. Testing by Which?, external shows it typically costs between 2p and 8p an hour to run an electric blanket at its highest setting. The London Fire Brigade, external says to unplug your blanket before you get into bed unless it has a thermostat control, not to use a hot water bottle at the same time, and replace it every 10 years.

Gaps around doors can cause heat to escape, so place draught excluders around your door frames. You don't need to buy them - you can use towels or stuff socks into a pair of tights.

When it's a windy day, Seymour recommends looking for other draughts in your house and either finding ways to seal these spots yourself or calling in a professional to help. These include using foam strips, sealant and specialist chimney draught excluders if you don't use your fireplace. Things such as extractor fans and purpose-built ventilation shouldn't be blocked, she adds.

If your windows are single-glazed, then Sophie Burr of charity National Energy Action suggests looking at secondary glazing or investing in thermal curtains to help keep the heat in. Or for a cheaper option, some people suggest placing bubble wrap on your windows.

Even though it may be tempting, don't keep your windows closed all the time. Seymour notes that it's important to allow some ventilation in your house to prevent damp.

"I wouldn't recommend not having your heating on at all," says Seymour, pointing to both the health issues this can cause as well as how pipes can freeze over.

But there are ways you can use heating wisely. These include checking whether your energy supplier offers cheaper prices at off-peak times, bleeding your radiators so that they're more efficient, and turning your heating up in small increments until you reach the right temperature. If you have furniture in front of your radiator, then try moving it to avoid blocking the heat.

You can also buy dedicated radiator foil or make your own with kitchen foil to reflect the heat back into the room rather than losing it through the walls, says Burr. She points out that about 35% of heat that comes from radiators is lost through walls.

Cora Harrison, 34, from Wakefield, says that she only turns the radiators on in the rooms her family is using and keeps the heating on at a low level when they're on holiday to avoid mould or pipes bursting. Some radiators have a snowflake symbol on the valve that activates the frost protection setting, meaning that if the room gets very cold, the radiator warms slightly to stop the pipes from bursting.

Another way to potentially reduce energy bills is to lower the flow temperature of your combi boiler. If you book a boiler service, an engineer can do this for you.

You can also find free warm spaces such as libraries and community centres in your area by looking online or contacting the council. Some spaces also provide free hot drinks.

Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical bill expected to jump by £276 a year, according to a forecast last month from consultancy Cornwall Insight. The 16% predicted increase would mark the biggest rise for four years.

Rising bills are "particularly concerning for people with kids, people with health conditions and the elderly," says Emily Jeremy, project manager at Manchester South Central Foodbank.

An estimated 9.4% of households in England lived in fuel poverty in 2025, according to the latest government figures, external.

Rodney Winchester, 65, from Thetford, who spoke to BBC News through the charity Christians Against Poverty, says he's "extremely worried" about rising energy prices. Because of health conditions, he says he has to keep the heating on throughout winter but is concerned he won't be able to afford it.

"It's so scary," Rodney says, adding that he's been cutting back on food spending and keeps getting ill in the cold weather.

If you are struggling with prices, the debt charity StepChange recommends checking whether you qualify for any additional support, like the Warm Home Discount and Winter Fuel Payment. It also advises contacting your energy supplier, which may be able to agree an affordable repayment plan or discuss support schemes.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Ruins of city hall a symbol of France divided by protests
BreakingNewsTab.text:
"It is a historical tragedy for France, not just Limoges".

Just six months into his mayoral term, it is hard to imagine Guillaume Guérin having a more momentous week.

We talk next to what became the defining image of last week's nationwide protests: the still impressive, yet fragile exterior of his town's 19th-Century town hall, charred from a fire.

The sight of its wooden clock tower collapsing into the flames drew widespread shock and anger, and Guérin, who was in tears when he first saw the scale of the damage this week, believes the reaction is "legitimate and completely understandable".

What is apparent from the array of flowers and sombre onlookers gathered at the hall's entrance, is that this is a town mourning the loss, or at the least the harm inflicted on its most iconic and, frankly, most beautiful building.

Guérin blames the damage on the French hard left, "supported by rioters". Two men have been arrested, a 66-year-old, as well as another suspect who is 34. Prosecutors say they have links to "radical-left networks".

Limoges' conservative mayor claims he has received a message of support from US Vice President JD Vance, but not Emmanual Macron, his own, outgoing president.

"What happened here will have an influence on the upcoming presidential election. This country is not doing well at all," he says.

For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a demonstration over the poor state of high schools has expanded to a general frustration, even anger, over how challenging and expensive life has become.

In the backdrop is a daunting fiscal deficit, one of the biggest in Europe, and political candidates from across the spectrum claiming to have the answers ahead of presidential elections in six months' time.

In the middle is a centrist government, which is short on solutions, a majority in the National Assembly and time. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu visited Limoges on Friday evening.

Officials have banned demonstrations in various cities and promised to boost police numbers over the weekend to avoid a repeat of the rioting. That includes in Limoges, where overnight curfews have been announced, along with a limit on gatherings to 10 people in the centre.

Proud as the French are of their politics being rooted in street demonstrations, many in Limoges felt the town hall's destruction went far beyond the parameters of reasonable protest. But not everyone.

Whether the destruction of Limoges town hall changes the course and tone of an increasingly polarised political debate depends on who you ask.

"Of course it was really sad, it's a symbol of the republic, but what is more important: a town hall or people living in poverty?" asks Alexander, 24.

It is student night at the Lord John pub, and Alexander is one of several wearing a faluche, a colourful, traditional French student beret. Many chatting under the mist from their vapes took part in the demonstrations last weekend.

I ask Alexander whether the widespread looting and fires seen last weekend, with €500,000 (£420,000) of reported damage in Limoges, helped his argument?

"For some people it's a catastrophe and some things are not acceptable," he admits.

Jade, a 19-year-old, medical student, has a similar opinion: "I think burning the town hall is sad, but it's not the saddest part of the protests."

She complains of having to live on €300 per month.

"I feel we are not respected as young adults."

Their views on the town hall's fate are not replicated in Limoges' imposing market halls, where neat, narrow timbers sitting upon studded steel girders have been painted a duck-egg blue, using the same engineering approach as the Eiffel Tower.

This has been a "week of chaos" that 63-year-old Jean Roger Faucher would like to forget.

In a region renowned for producing beef, his family has run his fishmonger stall here for more than a century.

"It left us stunned," he says. "I got married in the town hall, so it had an unimaginable effect on us."

Asked whether he had sympathy for the protesters, Faucher said it was more complicated than that.

"On one side you have people with grievances you can understand, but from the moment there is vandalism and the lives of local residents are put at risk, then we can't accept it," he adds.

Among those tending to their iced displays of fresh produce or quietly sipping a steaming coffee, there is a desire for the temperature of the demonstrations to decrease.

"Of course, life is expensive!' says Pascale Vuylsteke, 59. "Life isn't all a calm river, it's complicated, but we grit our teeth and we work," she tells me leaning over shelves of butchered pork.

Pascale says she works 100 hours a week and struggles to understand why so many others have taken to the streets so easily.

Limoges has found itself at the heart of social action before. In the 19th Century, around the time the town hall was built, the development of its industries, notably in porcelain, led to it becoming a major centre for the French labour movement.

In 2026, the town sits centre-stage once more in a political rupture, although there is a broad hope that the loss of a prominent piece of its history will steer the demonstrations away from destruction and back to debate.

With France's political polarisation set to continue and further protests planned, it is a scenario far from assured.

Additional reporting by Paul Pradier.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite internet network.

Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it.

This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back".

Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored.

"This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday.

Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield.

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues.

Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Fugitive fraudster Arif Patel from Preston stole £33m from public
BreakingNewsTab.text:
One of the UK's most prolific fraudsters, described by a judge as a "breathtakingly arrogant" and "totally dishonest" man, remains on the run in Dubai after stealing more than £33m of public money.

Arif Patel, from Preston in Lancashire, was exposed following a complex investigation spanning years, led by His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC), which established that he had tried to steal as much as £90m.

Patel, who skipped the UK in 2011 never to return, was eventually convicted in his absence and in 2023 was handed a 20-year prison sentence.

BBC File on 4 Investigates has been on the trail of the man who stole from all of us - and seemingly got away with it.

"Al Capone was brought down by the taxman. This is the same situation and 20 years was more than a satisfying result," said Rod Stone, a veteran investigator of large-scale tax fraud, of Patel's conviction and custodial sentence.

The judge at Patel's sentencing hearing described him as the leader of a "fraternal organised crime group" with his brothers Munaf and Faisal who were "truly high-level criminals".

The fact that Arif Patel has not served a single day of his 20-year prison sentence clearly rankles with Stone.

For him and the dozens of others who were involved in bringing Patel down, there remains a strong sense that justice has only been served on paper.

In the early part of the millennium, Arif Patel appeared to be a businessman very much on the up.

His company, Faisaltex, headquartered in his home city of Preston, was known for manufacturing textiles, such as socks and nighties, which it supplied to retailers.

Patel was a fixture in the Sunday Times Rich List with his wealth in 2006 estimated to be £105m. He was also investing heavily in property across the city and beyond.

In 2007, his teenage son bought a minority stake in Preston North End Football Club. There was even a plan to build a £100m, 19-storey tower block - complete with botanical gardens and restaurant - in the centre of the city.

Behind the facade, though, something very different was going on.

In the early 2000s, organised crime groups had turned to large-scale attacks on the tax system through what became known as carousel fraud.

Chains of fake business transactions are created as a way of stealing VAT repayments from HMRC.

Goods move between different companies, into and out of the country, to generate false tax refunds.

The same shipments of goods are often moved around repeatedly, hence the name carousel fraud.

This type of fraud was costing taxpayers billions of pounds a year and experts like Stone were at the vanguard of the fightback.

This is how Patel's textiles empire appeared on his radar.

"When we started to look at them we did notice some very strange shipments of goods - a container load of hats to Switzerland seemed odd because they were actually Swiss hats," he said.

Most carousel fraudsters dealt in high-value, high-volume items like mobile phones or computer chips, for which investigators were on the lookout.

But Patel's enterprise had predominantly been dealing in textiles, making the scam harder to spot.

The team of investigators discovered Patel had successfully stolen more than £33m of taxpayers' money before HMRC cottoned on to what he was doing.

In total, he tried to steal more than £90m of public money - the rest of the payments were stopped.

Teams of investigators spent years working through vast chains of transactions until they were ready to make their move.

Patel was charged with a range of offences including conspiracies to cheat the taxman, money-laundering, false accounting and selling counterfeit goods.

But when he appeared at Bolton Crown Court in 2011, Patel asked the judge for permission to travel to Dubai on bail.

The judge agreed to this request and Patel left the UK, never to return.

In Dubai, he joined his brothers Munaf and Faisal, who had already left the country before they could be charged for their part in the conspiracy.

Over the next three years, 24 members of Patel's gang were convicted. Collectively, they were jailed for more than 116 years.

Efforts to have Arif Patel extradited back to the UK failed and he remained a free man in Dubai.

The BBC has heard claims he had been actively seeking to strike a deal with the UK authorities to settle the case against him.

"In my opinion, he thought he was above justice," said Graham Honey, another former HMRC investigator.

In 2020, he was working in the private sector when he said he was approached by Patel's representatives.

Honey said he was asked to open up a channel of communication with HMRC and the Crown Prosecution Service because Patel wanted to make a deal.

It soon became clear, however, that there would be a sticking point.

"It started to become apparent to me that Patel was not willing to come back," said Honey.

"He just thought he could get an agreement, pay some money, and this would all go away."

Honey claimed that while Patel was willing to admit his guilt and repay money, he was not prepared to face a criminal trial or the prospect of time behind bars.

He claimed it was not the first time that Patel had attempted to strike such a deal.

Honey said: "One of the officers told me that he had said 'I'm a tiger, not a caged tiger' meaning he was a big man, he'd done what he'd done, but in essence, he wasn't prepared to go to prison for it."

In 2023, Patel's trial got under way without him, something which is highly unusual and only done as a last resort.

He was found guilty of leading one of the UK's biggest carousel fraud gangs and received a 20-year jail sentence.

In 2025, he was subjected to a confiscation order to repay £90.5m through the sale of assets found to have been gained through criminality.

The funds raised were to be returned to the public purse.

But more than a year later, none of the money has been recouped because, despite being on the run overseas, Patel has been able to go to the Court of Appeal to object to the confiscation order.

That matter has yet to be resolved.

So where is Patel now and what might he have done with his stolen millions?

The BBC has discovered that over the last few years, an increasing number of websites, press releases and social videos have begun to appear, celebrating the achievements of a businessman called Arif Patel in Dubai.

This Arif Patel is variously a business owner, an investor and a philanthropist. The photographs on the sites are often stock images or, in at least one case, belong to a different British entrepreneur.

Many of the pages also suggest Patel has links to Preston and worked in the textile industry.

The coincidences do not end there.

A story was published in 2024 in which Arif Patel denies allegations of fraud by HMRC.

The article quotes a "Sam Mackenzie", who it said was a close associate of Patel.

Mackenzie spoke out in support of Patel, whom he described as a "pillar of integrity".

The piece also said he had received backing from an "Andrew Fox", who the article described as having reviewed the claims and deemed them to be "unfounded".

It just so happens that the deputy chief constable of Lancashire police is called Sam Mackenzie, while Andrew Fox is a senior prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service.

Both men had been quoted in the media following Patel's conviction.

Their names appeared in other stories too, including one which claimed Patel had made a sizeable investment in HMRC anti-fraud technology in Lancashire.

The BBC does not know for certain whether Patel is connected to these sites, but File on 4 Investigates has established some sites are linked to an online reputation management company based in Dubai.

Another story was published earlier this year, this time about a donation Patel had made to a charitable organisation which supports children with disabilities in Dubai.

It shared similarities with some of the other websites but had one key difference - it featured a genuine photograph of Patel.

With an up-to-date picture, facial recognition technology uncovered numerous other pictures of Patel posing at glamorous events in Dubai.

We showed everything we had learned about the case to the prime minister's anti-corruption champion Dame Margaret Hodge.

"I think this is a shocking story of somebody who deliberately acted fraudulently and laundered money and he should be punished," she said.

"He should not be beyond the reach of the British justice system.

"I think he is clearly abusing the justice system in a way that only rich people can.

"There's an intrinsic injustice in a system that allows those with money to delay the implementation of a punishment for a crime and to delay the confiscation of assets which was stolen as part of that crime."

The BBC contacted the Government of Dubai but did not receive a response.

The BBC also contacted Arif Patel via his Manchester-based solicitor - as well as his brothers Munaf and Faisal - but did not hear back.

You can listen to the File on 4 Investigates at 20:00 GMT on Tuesday 27 October.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German manduring a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.

Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.

Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to the scene where the blaze was still burning early on Saturday, as police said difficult terrain hindered efforts to bring the fire under control.

Police said they apprehended the suspect riding a motorcycle near the scene and possible motives were still being examined, German media reported. A criminal investigation has been launched.

There is currently nothing to suggest the involvement of further suspects, police official Gerhart Holzinger told a press conference on Saturday afternoon.

Public prosecutor Rainer Vietze said a psychiatric report had concluded the 33-year-old man showed signs of possible mental illness and diminished responsibility might therefore be assumed.

Vietze said a possible political motive was also being considered, but stressed the investigation was in its early stages.

The residence, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.

Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.

He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.

Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed" and the public was urged to avoid the area.

Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann told reporters that the site would "under no circumstances remain a ruin", broadcaster BR24 reported. "It is important that we continue our work of remembrance," he added.

Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest, which sits at an elevation of around 1,800m (5,900ft), escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.

Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.

It serves as "a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship", according to its official website, external.

During WW2, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews. Homosexuals, gypsies, the disabled and ethnic minorities were sent to concentration camps and put to death.

There has been a wider debate in Germany and Vienna over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish buildings connected to Hitler.

While some say these buildings should be preserved for historical reasons, others have raised concerns that they could be used as monuments or places of pilgrimage for neo-Nazis and far-right extremists.

In June, Berlin authorities announced they would tear down one of Hitler's bunkers - described at the time as "the power centre of Nazi Germany" - to build flats and offices on the site.

Those critical of the plans said the bunker had "significant historical value" and that it should have been turned into a museum and memorial site with an exhibit about the end of the war.

And in July, after years of controversy, Austrian authorities refurbished the house in the town of Braunau am Inn in which Hitler was born and turned it into a police station.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Father who killed Oregon school gunman describes anguish over children he couldn't save
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A father who fatally shot a gunman at his daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described his anguish over being unable to save more pupils after "hearing children pleading for their lives".

Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month. The attacker was then killed by Kaylub Giamanco.

"I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed, in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday.

"The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."

Giamanco, 36, said he wanted to meet the victims' families and "cry with them and hold them".

He credited a teacher who fought the attacker with giving him the chance to intervene without losing his own life.

"I would love to give her a hug because that's a real true hero," he said.

The students who were killed were all boys, aged five, eight and 11. They were among six people in total who were shot in a classroom at the school, police said. Alongside the teacher who was killed, another child and a teacher were wounded.

Giamanco told OPB that the day of the attack began with breakfast and making packed lunches. He and his wife had spent extra time getting their daughters ready because it was school picture day.

The carpenter had taken lunch to work but decided to go home to eat with his wife instead. That decision brought him past the school as the attack began.

He initially wondered whether someone carrying a long gun was playing a prank. Then he saw him fire at a pickup truck and head towards the school.

Giamanco retrieved a handgun from his vehicle and called emergency services.

"I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die'," he told the broadcaster.

He followed the attacker, who shot through the school's locked glass doors. Hearing children pleading for their lives and more gunfire, Giamanco crawled towards the building.

"I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do," he said.

Giamanco crawled through a shattered window and reached the classroom, where a teacher was locked in a struggle with the gunman. He opened the door and fired.

Giamanco told OPB he fired again when the attacker reached for his weapon. He then placed his own gun on the ground and raised his hands as an officer appeared.

He described feeling like the "last line of defence" between the children and the gunman, and said he "was supposed to be there" that day.

Afterwards, he called his wife to say he would not be home for lunch and that she needed to get to the school immediately. He then called his mother to tell her what had happened.

"Mum, I just had to take the life of what I think is might be a child because he ran into my daughter's school with a gun," he said.

Police identified the gunman as Griffin J John II - a former pupil who had attended special education classes at the school. His motive remains under investigation.

Police said the teacher who confronted the attacker had thrown her phone at him, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".

The youngest victim was Rhoam Summer, aged five. His father said the family was "broken and lost".

Megan Lambert, 25, the teacher who was killed, was working in what her family described as her "dream job".

"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.

The other two boys have not been publicly named at their families' request.

The injured teacher has been named as Becky Drury, 54. She said in a statement shared with US media that the gunman shot her as she tried to shut her classroom door.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election
BreakingNewsTab.text:
If Sunday's parliamentary elections really are a battle for the heart of Serbia, then who better than a cardiologist to be one of the leading figures in the race.

Ilija Srdanović appears an unlikely opponent for Serbia's long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vučić, arriving for an interview by motorbike sporting a fluorescent yellow jacket emblazoned with pro-student slogans.

He has been selected as top candidate for an opposition movement posing the most serious challenge to Vučić since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) entered government in 2012.

The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests led by young Serbians, outraged by the deaths of 16 people when a railway station's canopy collapsed in Serbia's second city Novi Sad.

The Student List is up against a Serbian leader who has served successively as deputy prime minister, prime minister and president since 2012. When he called these snap elections last month, he stood down as president to run again for the role of prime minister.

Whatever Vučić's title, there has never been any doubt that he was the man in charge – an image enthusiastically promoted by Serbia's largely uncritical media.

He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure.

Vučić has painted the student movement as foreign-backed and seeking to "bring down our state". "Let us always protect and defend it," he told supporters at a final campaign rally.

Just like the protest movement from which it developed, the Student List has no hierarchy or nominated leader. This makes it a proposition unlike any other in Serbia's relatively short democratic history.

Reliable polls are thin on the ground, but analysts are predicting an extremely tight vote.

Ilija Srdanović may head the list of candidates – but he is not the movement's leader and would not necessarily be first choice prime minister if they won.

Srdanović insists that the Student List has a clear vision: "We offer to our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time."

The other candidates on the Student List range from academics to athletes – and economists to engineers. None of them has a political background. But the students who selected them believe that is a strength, rather than a weakness.

"We've gathered people who are actually the best in their fields, and we really think that they are competent enough to rule the country," says Aleksandra, a student at Novi Sad University who only wants to give her first name.

"All of them are gathered around the same vision of a country where the freedom of speech is ruling, where you can walk to your home in the middle of the night and you will not be beaten up by some hooligans," she adds.

The Student List and its supporters say that Aleksandar Vučić and the SNS dominate state institutions and media coverage.

At the last parliamentary election in 2023, the International Election Observation Mission noted "overwhelming ruling party advantage" due to "bias in the media" and "misuse of public office and resources".

The BBC approached leading figures in the SNS for an interview but was not offered a response.

Protests followed, with participants accusing the authorities of corruption and having "blood on their hands".

"This is a problem for the government," says Magda Anastasijevic, the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor, ACLED.

"Vučić has survived this in the past, he was always able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy."

On the diplomatic front, he has performed a delicate balancing act.

Membership talks with the EU continue, albeit fitfully, even as Serbia retains close ties with Russia and China – both countries that refuse to recognise Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.

Vučić has warned those links could be severed if the Student List took power.

"When you ask them: will you impose sanctions on Russia? Silence, umming and ah-ing, but no answer," he told the audience at a pre-election rally.

"You know what the Chinese think, you've heard what Vladimir Putin said. So you decide. Think about who has our best interests at heart."

The final rallies of the campaign saw the SNS stage an event at Belgrade Arena, with Aleksandar Vučić as the only speaker. But on the other side of the Sava River, the Student List attracted a reported 150,000 people in Slavija Square to listen to a mixture of students and candidates.

The contrasting visions were clear to see: the strong, sole leader – or a collective approach. Now Serbia's electorate must decide which they prefer.
